items.title:
Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf.

A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser,
items.content:
Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf.

A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser, network, filesystem, system fonts. Renders a post to PNG in ~1ms (and 0.4 ms for @jack's "setting up my twttr" 😁).

X is the global town square, and the medium is the message. Being able to preview what things will look like before posting is great for both humans and agents.

Rendering with xeet is is 100x-1000x faster than booting up a browser and taking a screenshot, yet it's just as accurate.

It reproduces Blink & HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64px line breaking, RTL bidi, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK/Math/Emoji fallbacks, "Show more" rules, etc. It's the kind of thing that would be wildly impractical, if not impossible, for a human engineer to pull off.

Except 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝 is structured as an "autorepo." An oracle boots up Chrome, and verifies tens of thousands of text layout rules. A CI canary then watches the evolution of the original, and files signed PRs for agents to act on. It was conceived from the ground up around 'verification engineering', and the result speaks for itself.

Enjoy!

items.content:
Google DeepMind's Alex Imas says AI agents still struggle to coordinate, and that's a key bottleneck to economic transformation:

"What you actually need for real economic transformation is not just competence... It's the ability of these agents to coordinate with one another."

"There's this idea of agentic swarms, right? But if you unpack it, these agents are still very bad at coordinating. They're not coordinating, they're mostly just doing parallel processing."

"If you have benchmarks specifically on coordination, you could actually show that 1 agent does better than 2 agents splitting the work, even if they can communicate. Whereas if you give the same thing to people, they actually have division of labor, they communicate, and they do way better than 1 person with double the resources."

"But if they get better at coordinating, you can basically break the Coasean ceiling on firm size, and you can get very, very different firms to emerge."

"Once coordination becomes better, the economic space of possibilities of what firms look like, what happens to wages, what happens to employment, that's when the real kind of visible changes are going to happen."

items.title: I send around PDFs and markdown files to my coworkers so much and they use their agents to make sense of the world too,
items.content:
I send around PDFs and markdown files to my coworkers so much and they use their agents to make sense of the world too, so I started using this skill methodology-appendix to make sure their agents could replicate what my agents found. 

---
name: methodology-appendix
description: "Every data-backed report or memo ends with a Methodology / Replication Appendix: the signal choice and its sensitivity, verbatim queries, derivation pseudocode over named constants, the rebuild command, and drift/limits. Appended by default, without asking."
---

# Methodology / Replication Appendix

## Rule

Any report, PDF or page whose conclusions rest on data queries ends with a
**Replication Appendix**. It is a working recipe, not a citation list. The test:

> A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate the document
> end to end from the appendix alone, without contacting the author.

If a reader would have to ask "which column did you use?", "what date was this
pulled?" or "how do I rebuild the PDF?", the appendix failed.

## Body voice

The body states conclusions plainly. No process narration ("I was asked...",
"on the first pass..."), no self-grading. The first sentence after the title
contains a finding. Everything about how you got there goes in the appendix at
the end, written for forensic recreation.

## When this fires

Always, automatically, for:
- analysis memos backed by database or API queries
- any PDF sent to partners, executives or external stakeholders
- pages presenting quantitative findings
- anything with tables of counts, rates or percentiles

Skip for narrative or qualitative writing, meeting notes, personal memos,
short ephemera, and documents with no data spine. Do not ask permission.

## The six sections

### 1. Header

```markdown
## Replication Appendix

A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate every number
and rebuild this document from this appendix alone.

**Access required:** <tool/CLI + auth, internal APIs>
**Snapshot date:** <ISO date>. Live-data documents won't reproduce exactly after this date; see Drift.
```

### 2. Signal definitions and the choice that mattered

The most important section. Analyses usually turn on one column or threshold
choice. Name it, name the alternatives, state the impact.

```markdown
### Signal definitions

| Field | What it is | Why chosen / rejected |
|---|---|---|
| `score_a` | Ensembled score | **Primary.** More predictive per <source>. |
| `score_b` | Single-model score | Rejected as primary; kept for contrast. |
| final_decision | Human decision object | Not queried. Known gap. |

**Outcome sensitivity:** switching from score_b to score_a moved the headline
count from N1 to N2 and changed claim X. A replication that changes the signal
column will not match these numbers.
```

Always include an **Outcome sensitivity** line. If a different defensible choice
changes the conclusion, the reader must know before quoting it.

### 3. Verbatim queries

Every query that produced a number, copy-pasteable, in document order, labelled
by the finding it supports. Never paraphrase SQL. Never write "similar to the
above." Add schema notes a replicator would otherwise get wrong: enum meanings,
non-obvious joins, columns that seem to exist but don't.

### 4. Derivation pseudocode

Queries give raw counts; the document has derived figures. Show the arithmetic,
with assumptions as named constants a reader can swap.

```
ITEMS_PER_DAY   = 8        # observed median, <period>
YIELD_HAIRCUT   = 0.10..0.15   # marginal cases convert below observed rate

gap          = count(status = REJECTED and score >= threshold)
extra_days   = gap / ITEMS_PER_DAY
added_wins   = gap * YIELD_HAIRCUT
```

Different constants change the recommendation, not just the number, so they
must be visible.

### 5. Rebuild command

Exact commands from source markdown to verified PDF, plus a visual check
(e.g. `pdfinfo` page count, `pdftoppm` a couple of pages and look at them).
Name the source of record: the PDF is a render, never the original.

### 6. Drift, limits and known gaps

- **Live data moves.** What was mid-flight at snapshot; what is closed and stable.
- **Coverage gaps.** Fields only populated for part of the range, and how tables were restricted rather than shown with misleading denominators.
- **What this cannot see.** Inputs to the real decision that the data lacks.
- **Retractions.** Any claim withdrawn between versions, and why.

## Procedure

1. Log queries verbatim as you run them. Reconstructed SQL is how appendices go wrong.
2. Write the analysis.
3. Append the six sections before rendering.
4. Name the signal choice and its outcome sensitivity.
5. Render, check visually, then send.
6. On revision, update the appendix in the same commit as the finding. An appendix describing a superseded method is worse than none.

## Quality bar

- [ ] Could a reader re-run this without asking me anything?
- [ ] Is every headline number traceable to a pasted query?
- [ ] Is the signal/threshold choice named, with alternatives and impact?
- [ ] Are derived figures arithmetic over named constants?
- [ ] Is the rebuild command present and correct?
- [ ] Are drift, coverage gaps and retractions stated?

## Anti-patterns

- **Citation theater:** table names instead of runnable queries.
- **Reconstructed SQL:** retyped from memory, drifted from what ran.
- **Silent signal choice:** one column presented as "the score" when a defensible alternative changes the answer.
- **Buried assumptions:** constants hard-coded in prose.
- **Stale appendix:** findings revised, appendix untouched.
- **Asking first:** this is a default, not an offer.

"Good matches will be harder. Search will take longer. I don't think that problem will be with us forever. Eventually, the AIs themselves will figure it out, and there'll be certifications for how good a person is in AI."

"But in the transition, everyone's a novice. You might be well-established the way a lot of people in the tech world are, but otherwise, we're all novices at this very important new skill."

items.title: I think the explosion of “neolabs” in quantitative trading has been brought about by a misconception either in the compe
items.content:
I think the explosion of “neolabs” in quantitative trading has been brought about by a misconception either in the competitive landscape OR where money is made in quantitative trading.

The idea that a startup claims to be the first to pursue “the bitter lesson” in quantitative trading is absolutely ludicrous. 

Top tier quant funds have long been hiring AI researchers and training end-to-end (industry parlance: tick-to-trade) models for years. From memory: HRT, UbiQuant, XTX, HighFlyer (hello, deepseek?!), and many, many, many more.

In every podshop, there is at least 1 team with a focus on creating large scale end-to-end models that “train on markets directly”.

If you CLAIM to be the first, you either don’t understand the landscape or are straight up lying, or don’t even have the slightest clue on the SOTA problems being worked on by your past employers.

—

I can’t speak to their skills, but there is some insinuation here that training the largest model and throwing a lot of data at the model will “solve” quantitative trading.

Markets are for better or worse, reflexive. That makes it hard for anyone to achieve high predictive power for a long time. Research is almost always a constant race to maintain your position - unlike more general machine learning, there is no evidence that SoTA models in markets have been able to continuously improve their predictive power beyond a certain threshold.

The implication here is that money is often made not purely from the models, but also the non-trivial technological and operational scaffold of being able to monetise low signal-to-noise models.

Spoken plainly, there is a lot of work to be done across the entire investment process in order for a single dollar to be generated. 

When one has been a fledgling researcher, he is tasked only to focus on and think about the model. And upon any initial success, he is almost always convinced that his portion is the lion’s share of the work, oblivious to the thousand moving parts that made his model work.

items.content:
I found a way to trick AI detectors, so everything is 100% human-generated. I’ll teach you how, but also why you must never do it:

Step 1. Open Claude.

Ask for 50 common kitchen words, starting with “chicken, rice, salt, pepper”. Just random words in no particular order.

Step 2. Put the list into Pangram .com (the only AI detector I trust, it's also free to use).

I got that list labeled as 100% AI-generated. 

Step 3. Ask Claude to give you another list.

Test it again. It will still be 100% AI-generated. 

Step 4. Write 50 words yourself manually and check in Pangram. It will be 100% human-written.

Step 5. Now, go to https://t.co/ZIRK9FXG3m

Copy the long Wikipedia prompt & paste it into Claude. It restricts Claude to only write using the sentences and words mentioned in the Wikipedia article. 

Step 6. Copy the Claude response and put it into Pangram. I bet, it will give you 100% human-written.

Hold on, before you call this a writing hack:

Claude wrote existing human-written text. It straight up copied from another work. But YOU got the label of 'human-written'. You're still not the author of that writing piece.

Step 7. The point is far from taking someone else's work and asking Claude to rewrite it.

In that case, you do not own any writing piece Claude gives you. You are better off writing by yourself.

Writing is thinking. As simple as that.
Research & write with AI (without giving the ick).
And it's okay if you used AI & it’s 100% AI-detected.

Conclusion: AI is not the best at writing (it sounds crazy). But if you should be using AI, it’s actually to code without knowing how to code.

So, close Claude & Pangram. Instead, open a Google Doc. And write something you are actually thinking.

items.title:
An Anthropic engineer just showed how the Claude Code team actually uses Claude now. 

Most of you are still doing it th
items.content:
An Anthropic engineer just showed how the Claude Code team actually uses Claude now. 

Most of you are still doing it the old way.

Lydia Hallie works on Claude Code at Anthropic. She just gave away the tricks her team uses every day. This is the stuff you won't find in any tutorial.

1. Delete "IMPORTANT!" from your CLAUDE.md
With today's models, lines like "IMPORTANT" or "NEVER do this!" can push Claude off track. You get more tool calls and worse results.

Keep only what Claude can't see in your code, like a service that still depends on some legacy source. Your stack and folder layout don't need to be there.

Run /doctor prompt-audit and it checks your CLAUDE.md and skills for what the current model no longer needs

2. Stop approving every command
Auto mode is the default since August. If it still asks too often, open settings and write in plain English which repos, buckets and domains you trust. That text goes straight to the classifier

3. Add deny rules for what can't be undone
In Anthropic's study only about 14% of people caught a clearly dangerous command. Auto mode blocked 89%. But about 1 in 10 still went through.

Ask yourself one question. If Claude gets this wrong once, can I take it back? Wrong code you can revert. A leaked key or lost uncommitted work you can't, so those get a deny rule.

Deny rules are checked before the classifier even sees the command

4. Turn on the sandbox
A normal npm test runs code you didn't write. A compromised dependency could read your .env or SSH keys and send them somewhere.

Permissions can't stop that. The sandbox can, because the operating system blocks it, even for every process the command starts.

By default it can still read most of your machine, so add a rule for your SSH keys too.

5. Run long tasks in the cloud

A cloud session gets its own machine with a fresh copy of the repo. Your .env, SSH keys and tokens aren't there. Network is limited to package registries and GitHub. It keeps working when you close your laptop.

Keep auto mode and deny rules there too. The machine is disposable, a pushed commit isn't.

6. Add checkpoints, not just a final review
Tell Claude what done looks like, ask it to split the work into tasks with their own tests, and make it show the actual output.

For checks that must always run, use hooks. Linter on every edit, tests when a task is done, the full suite before the session ends.

One detail most people miss. Make your hook scripts exit with code 2. With exit code 1 Claude Code marks the task complete anyway.

7. Let CI be the bar for every session
Every session opens a PR and CI runs the same checks on all of them. CI auto-fix sends Claude back when something fails.

At Anthropic every PR is reviewed by Claude first, in a fresh context. Docs and copy changes need no human. Normal changes get one reviewer, risky ones get two.

8. Talk to one session instead of eight
In Claude Code projects (still in beta) one main session splits the work, starts other sessions and checks what comes back. She uses Fable for the main session and Opus 5.5 for the workers. Context is managed automatically.

Working like this, Anthropic went from about 2,500 changes a day in May to over 30,000 a day in September.

items.content:
Stop installing Claude Code skills blind. In a study of 31,132, 1 in 4 had a security hole.

The most common one sends your data somewhere else. NVIDIA built a free scanner on that research, and it checks a skill before you install it.

Skills are the add-ons you drop into Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI. They run with implicit trust and minimal vetting.

That data leak turned up in 13.3% of them. Another 5.2% had high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent. Skills that ship their own scripts were 2.12x more likely to be vulnerable.

A fake Claude Code extension already sat where real users download them. On Oct 29 an attacker used a credential stolen from Cursor to slip tampered copies of Anthropic's official build into Cursor's marketplace. Anthropic never published them. They stayed up about 11 hours, and up to 5,000 people may have received one. Cursor warns that uninstalling alone may not be enough.

SkillSpector covers skills, not extensions:
- 71 attack patterns in 17 categories, from prompt injection to memory poisoning
- Takes a GitHub link, a folder, a zip or a single SKILL.md
- Returns a 0-100 risk score and a verdict of SAFE, CAUTION or DO NOT INSTALL

Two lines in your terminal:
uv tool install git+https://t.co/E2U2R5MAQH
skillspector scan https://t.co/7i5BMIPcgy --no-llm

Swap in the real link. The --no-llm flag keeps the skill's code on your machine instead of sending it to an AI server.

How many skills did you install this month without opening a single file?
